summary: A Segment Routing Policy is an ordered list of instructions defining a source-routed path, with candidate paths. This RFC specifies how to advertise SR Policies in BGP so headends can be given them rather than only through local configuration.

eli5.summary: A trip plan is a list of stops. This lets BGP deliver trip plans to routers.

questions: how to advertise segment routing policy
what is an sr policy in bgp
what is a segment list sub-tlv
what is the color extended community
subtitle: How BGP carries Segment Routing candidate paths to the routers that will steer traffic along them.

tldr.problem: A Segment Routing Policy is an ordered list of segments that defines a source-routed path. A headend router can learn its candidate paths by CLI, NETCONF or PCEP, but there was no BGP way to distribute them.
tldr.mechanism: A new SR Policy SAFI (73) carries an NLRI of Distinguisher, Color and Endpoint. The path details ride in the Tunnel Encapsulation Attribute as an SR Policy tunnel type (15) with sub-TLVs for preference, binding SID, segment lists and more.
tldr.outcome: BGP only originates and propagates these candidate paths. The SR Policy Module on the headend validates and uses them. The RFC also updates RFC 9012 by adding Color-Only bits to the Color Extended Community.

today: RFC 9830 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2025. It updates RFC 9012, and no later RFC is recorded as updating or obsoleting it.

sections.title: Delivering SR Policies with BGP
sections.content:
Segment Routing (RFC 8402) lets a headend node steer a packet flow along a specific path by putting an ordered list of segments on the packet. This removes per-path state from intermediate nodes. The concepts of an SR Policy and of steering into one are detailed in RFC 9256.

An SR Policy has one or more candidate paths (CPs). On the headend, an SR Policy Module (SRPM) learns CPs from several sources (CLI, NETCONF, PCEP or BGP), selects the best one, associates a Binding SID with it and installs it in the forwarding plane. This RFC covers the BGP source only.

BGP does not install SR Policy CPs in the data plane. It uses the usual BGP propagation and best-path rules, and then hands the paths in its table to the SRPM. Typically a controller advertises policies to headends, often over a direct BGP session. Where that is impractical, route reflectors can propagate them, with Route Target extended communities identifying the intended headends.
sections.eli5: Think of a delivery truck that follows a list of stops. A boss (the controller) writes the list, and BGP is the mail carrier that brings it to the truck. The truck's own driver decides whether to use it.

sections.title: The SR Policy SAFI and NLRI
sections.content:
The SR Policy SAFI has code point 73 and is used with AFI 1 (IPv4) or 2 (IPv6). Its NLRI has four parts: a 1-octet NLRI Length in bits, a 4-octet Distinguisher, a 4-octet Color and an Endpoint of 4 or 16 octets. The length value MUST be 96 for AFI 1 and 192 for AFI 2.

The Distinguisher has no meaning of its own. It lets an originator form unique NLRIs for several CPs of the same policy, or for CPs meant for different headends that share a Color and Endpoint. The Color is a non-zero unsigned integer used to match traffic to the policy. The Endpoint is a unicast address or a null address (0.0.0.0 or ::).

If several CPs of one policy reach a headend, each NLRI SHOULD be different in its Distinguisher (the RFC says RECOMMENDED). BGP passes each to the SRPM with the originator's ASN and a BGP Router-ID, taken from the Route Origin Community, else the ORIGINATOR_ID, else the peer's Router-ID. The next hop can be an IPv4 or IPv6 address regardless of the AFI.
sections.eli5: Each trip plan gets an address label with three parts: a ticket number to tell copies apart, a color that says what kind of traffic it is for, and the place it ends.

sections.title: The Tunnel Encapsulation Attribute and Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
The CP's content is carried in the Tunnel Encapsulation Attribute (RFC 9012) using a tunnel type called "SR Policy", code point 15. It applies only to AFI/SAFI pairs 1/73 and 2/73. Using any other tunnel type with this SAFI, or more than one SR Policy TLV in the attribute, is malformed and handled as treat-as-withdraw (RFC 7606). The Tunnel Egress Endpoint and Color sub-TLVs from RFC 9012 are ignored here.

The policy details are optional sub-TLVs. Preference (type 12), Binding SID (13), SRv6 Binding SID (20), Explicit NULL Label Policy (14) and Priority (15) are single-purpose items. The Segment List (128), Candidate Path Name (129) and Policy Name (130) use a 2-octet length, since code points of 128 or higher get that. Names should be limited to 255 bytes.

The Binding SID sub-TLV has S and I flags (Specified-BSID-Only and Drop-Upon-Invalid). Its length is 2, 6 or 18 depending on whether it holds no BSID, an SR-MPLS label or an SRv6 SID. Implementations are told to prefer the SRv6 Binding SID sub-TLV for SRv6, which adds a B flag and an optional behavior and structure block of 8 octets. None of these sub-TLVs affect BGP best-path selection; they go to the SRPM.
sections.eli5: The trip plan is written on a form with optional boxes: how important the plan is, a special parking spot number, a name, and the list of stops. BGP just carries the form without reading the details.

sections.title: Segment Lists and Segments
sections.content:
A Segment List sub-TLV encodes one explicit path toward the Endpoint. It may appear several times in an SR Policy encoding, and the order does not matter. It holds an optional single Weight sub-TLV (type 9, a 4-octet unsigned value where zero is invalid) and zero or more Segment sub-TLVs.

RFC 9256 defines segment types A to K. This RFC specifies only Type A (type 1, one SR-MPLS label with TC, S and TTL fields) and Type B (type 13, one 16-octet SRv6 SID with an optional 8-octet behavior and structure block). The other types are in RFC 9831. A mix of SR-MPLS and SRv6 segments makes a segment list invalid.

In Type A, the S bit must be zero on transmission. A TC of zero or a TTL of 255 asks the receiver to choose the value, and the receiver may override the originator's values by local policy. The segment Flags carry a V flag (SID verification) and a B flag (behavior and structure present). The four length fields of the structure block must add up to 128 bits or less.
sections.eli5: A segment list is the list of stops on one route. Each stop can have a weight, like how many of the trucks should take this route.

sections.title: The Color Extended Community
sections.content:
The Color Extended Community from RFC 9012 is how BGP service routes are matched to an SR Policy with the same Color. It may appear in updates for IPv4 and IPv6 unicast, labeled unicast, VPN labeled unicast and EVPN.

This RFC updates RFC 9012 by using the two leftmost bits of the Flags field as a Color-Only Type. They say how the route's BGP next hop should match the policy Endpoint. One or more Color communities may be on a route.
sections.eli5: A color sticker on a package says which trip plan to use. The two special marks say how strict the match is: exact destination only, or also a catch-all.

sections.title: Advertising, Validating and Propagating SR Policies
sections.content:
A controller or PCE usually computes the policy, and a BGP speaker originates it. One or more route targets SHOULD be attached, each naming intended headends. If none is attached, the update goes directly to the receiver and the NO_ADVERTISE community MUST be attached.

On receipt, a speaker checks that the NLRI is 12 or 24 octets, that the update has NO_ADVERTISE or at least one IPv4-format Route Target, and that a Tunnel Encapsulation Attribute with the SR Policy tunnel type is present. Otherwise the update is malformed and is not passed to the SRPM.

A valid update is usable only if a route target matches the receiver's BGP Identifier, or if it has NO_ADVERTISE and no route target. An update with an unrecognized sub-TLV SHOULD NOT be considered usable. NO_ADVERTISE updates are never propagated. By default nothing is sent to EBGP neighbors, and IBGP follows normal rules. The SR Policy information in the attribute must not be altered.
sections.eli5: Each plan has a note saying which trucks it is for. A truck only uses a plan marked for it, and plans marked private are not passed on to anyone else.

sections.title: Error Handling
sections.content:
Errors follow RFC 7606. Malformed NLRIs that can be skipped are treated as withdrawn. If an encoding error stops the whole update being processed, the router SHOULD disable the AFI/SAFI when other families run on the session, or otherwise MUST reset the session. Any error in the Tunnel Encapsulation Attribute or its sub-TLVs causes treat-as-withdraw, since the update would not be usable.

BGP must not check the meaning of the sub-TLV fields. That belongs to the SRPM. Errors SHOULD be logged.
sections.eli5: If a plan is written wrong, it is treated as if it was never sent. Only if the whole mailbag is jumbled does the carrier stop that mail route.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The base BGP security model applies. SR operates within a trusted SR domain, and SR Policies distributed by BGP are expected to stay within it: a single AS or several ASes within one provider network. The RFC suggests isolating SR Policy SAFI sessions so policies are not sent by mistake to an EBGP peer outside the domain.

Exporting SR Policy information could also expose sensitive details such as endpoint addresses, SIDs and deployed policies. Operators must configure only trusted routers and controllers to receive it.
sections.eli5: Trip plans are private. Only trusted trucks and bosses inside the company should get them.

fields.name: Distinguisher
fields.desc: Tells apart CPs of the same policy or for different headends.

fields.name: Color
fields.desc: Non-zero value used to match steered traffic.

fields.name: Endpoint
fields.desc: IPv4 address (4 octets); 16 octets for IPv6.

children.label: SR Policy Name, Candidate Path Name, ENLP

items.label: Binding SID
items.desc: BSID for SR-MPLS or SRv6; flags S and I.

items.label: Priority
items.desc: Order of recomputation after topology change.

items.label: SRv6 Binding SID
items.desc: SRv6 BSID with optional behavior and structure.

items.label: Segment List
items.desc: One explicit path; holds Weight and Segment sub-TLVs.

items.label: Candidate Path Name
items.desc: Symbolic name of the candidate path.

items.label: Policy Name
items.desc: Symbolic name of the SR Policy.

items.label: Specific Endpoint Match
items.desc: Match the Endpoint that is the BGP next hop.

items.label: Specific or Null Endpoint Match
items.desc: Match the next-hop Endpoint or a null Endpoint.

items.label: Specific, Null, or Any Endpoint Match
items.desc: Match the next-hop, a null or any Endpoint.

items.label: Reserved
items.desc: Should not be used; treated like Type 0 on reception.

items.label: IPv4 only
items.desc: Push IPv4 Explicit NULL on unlabeled IPv4 packets, not IPv6.

items.label: IPv6 only
items.desc: Push IPv6 Explicit NULL on unlabeled IPv6 packets, not IPv4.

items.label: Both
items.desc: Push Explicit NULL on both unlabeled IPv4 and IPv6 packets.

items.label: None
items.desc: Do not push an Explicit NULL label.
